extracted.intended_audience: business owners, industrial managers, and entrepreneurs interested in production and financial policy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and evaluative criteria for running a manufacturing business, covering finance, production efficiency, personnel, pricing, inventory, and broader monetary/ social policy views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worst time to borrow money is when bankers think you need money
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not borrow when banking people or the market perceive that you need money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bankers think you need money you are in a weak negotiating position; borrowing then can saddle a business with debt that diminishes incentive to improve production. Example: bankers offering loans often want to insert their own treasurer to take control of finance rather than suggest engineering or production improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find resources within the business instead of borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before resorting to external credit, search the business itself for capital by cutting waste, selling unneeded assets, collecting receivables, and speeding up operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford's example: sold stock on hand, collected foreign accounts, sold by-products, sped up transit to free inventory capital, and sold Liberty Bonds—together turning $20M cash into $87.3M. Specific actions included shutting down for house-cleaning, selling useless assets, and reorganizing operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: House-cleaning: eliminate everything that doesn’t contribute to production
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove departments, processes, forms, personnel, and activities that do not directly aid in the production of the company's primary product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cut office forces in half, convert office workers to shop jobs where appropriate, abolish unused order blanks and statistics, reduce telephone extensions by 60%, and reduce foremen ratio from 1:5 to 1:20. Measure by effect on overhead per unit (Ford cut overhead from $146 to $93 per car).

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything and everybody must produce or get out
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a strict productivity standard: retain only personnel and processes that demonstrably contribute to output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule was applied to both shop and office staff; 'ceasing to be unproductive' could mean reassignment rather than firing. The aim is to reduce unproductive labor while preserving productive employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed up turnover to reduce capital needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorten the manufacturing cycle and logistics time so inventory investment and interest costs fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reducing cycle from 22 to 14 days released significant capital—Ford computed $28M released and $1.2M annual interest saved. Faster freight and improved transit were key levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut prices to stimulate demand and force market adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Make decisive price cuts—even below current production cost on older inventory—to expand demand, realign prices to 'natural' levels, and accelerate industry-wide adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford cut the touring car price from $575 to $440 to create a sensation and move prices down quickly rather than protract a depression. Accept short-term loss to accelerate recovery and increase longer-term production and employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate waste rather than rely on wage cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce unit costs by removing inefficiencies and overheads rather than primarily cutting workers’ wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford emphasizes that cuts in overhead and process inefficiency can lower prices while preserving employment and boosting production. Example: lowering overhead per car rather than reducing wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing bankers to control industrial management
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist putting financial controllers (bank-appointed treasurers) in charge of industrial operations; banking perspectives focus on money not production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bankers think of factories as money-making devices and prioritize credit control; their insertion can prevent needed engineering and production improvements. Banks should be servants of industry, not its masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer productive fixes (engineering, methods) over financial fixes (loans)
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing a shortfall, prioritize improving production methods and reducing costs instead of using credit to paper over problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford argues that borrowing would have removed the pressure to find methods to cheapen production, leaving the company with higher per-unit costs (estimated ~$4 per car in interest) and less competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money should be stable — a dollar must be a dollar
rubrics_metrics.description: A stable medium of exchange is essential; frequent changes in the purchasing power of money undermine trust and economic functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford critiques fluctuating valuations (e.g., 100-cent dollar becoming 65-, 50-, 47-cent dollar) and sees sound money as analogous to fixed measures (foot, pound). He cautions against sensational political solutions and urges public education on money.

rubrics_metrics.name: The financial system must not favor one class of producers
rubrics_metrics.description: A good monetary/credit system should not confer structural advantages to particular classes or interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford sees the gold standard and current credit controls as giving class advantage and calls for reform to take power away from those whose control is not based on wealth creation. He opposes 'class legislation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform banking/credit by cautious, well-founded experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to the monetary system should be incremental and experimentally tested rather than dogmatic or purely political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford rejects dogmatism about money; advocates step-by-step cautious experiments and public education so people won't be misled into harmful policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cure poverty by better production and distribution, not by forced leveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate poverty through increasing production and improving distribution and methods, rather than by leveling down or coercive equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford argues production science and intelligent leadership will allow abundance; forced equality reduces efficiency. Emphasizes preventing waste and better adjustment between production and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in human capital and productive use rather than hoarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage investment in self-improvement and productive ventures over mere saving for its own sake, especially for young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford suggests young men should invest in themselves to become more productive rather than simply saving; overemphasis on thrift can 'prevent becoming more productive' and is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix seasonal farm and factory work to remove slack times
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate labor between farming and manufacturing so workers move seasonally between occupations, smoothing employment and better using skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: builders work on farms in off-season; farmers come into factories in dull farm seasons. This teamwork reduces unemployment, broadens workers' experience, and balances community life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify product lines — adhere to the single-product principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the enterprise focused on a single primary product to avoid wasteful complexity introduced by diversions (e.g., wartime work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford notes war work forced departure from single-product principle, adding departments and waste; returning to single-product focus simplifies management and reduces inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect only statistics that directly aid production
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid accumulating interesting but useless statistics; retain only those metrics that directly inform production decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford recounts abolishing many forms and statistics because 'statistics will not construct automobiles'—focus measurement on what contributes to output and decision-making.
